newsitem.title: USA: Salinger stands by TWA remarks, meets FBI.
newsitem.headline: Salinger stands by TWA remarks, meets FBI.

text.p: Former White House official Pierre Salinger, who created a storm last week when he suggested the U.S. government covered up charges that a Navy missile accidentally destroyed TWA Flight 800, said on Tuesday he stood by his remarks and would later meet the FBI.

Crash investigators angrily denounced Salinger's remarks in France last Thursday and Friday as "unadulterated nonsense". Salinger acknowledged his information was at least second hand and had been on the Internet for months.

"I have been pretty well attacked around the world for what I said about the TWA 800 flight," Salinger said before a speech on Tuesday afternoon to the International Travel Professionals group in Boston. "For the moment, I am still believing what I said is correct."
"If what I said turns out to be wrong, it will probably be the biggest mistake of my entire life."
"If I do make that mistake, it'll be the first mistake I've made since the 1930s or the early 1940s," he said.

Salinger, 71, who was President John F. Kennedy's press secretary and later became Paris bureau chief for the ABC television network, said on Thursday he had been given a government document that he believed proved a U.S. missile accidentally shot down the Paris-bound Boeing 747 off Long Island on July 17, killing all 230 people on board.
Salinger, whose Boston speech was entitled "The New World Disorder" said he met with the FBI in Paris on Saturday and would meet the FBI in New York later on Tuesday.

In New York, FBI spokesman Joe Valiquette confirmed that FBI agents were expecting to meet with Salinger. "We anticipate he will be meeting with us. We don't anticipate making any statement about it," the spokesman said.

The latest version of an alleged cover-up conspiracy theory that has circulated on the Internet and in other media for months -- and was repeatedly denied by authorities -- erupted at a time when some investigators leaned toward ruling out sabotage and declaring the disaster an accident.

However, senior FBI and National Transportation Safety Board investigators have consistently identified three possible causes of the disaster -- a bomb, a missile or catastrophic mechanical failure -- and have not reached any definitive conclusion.
